source.title: Automatic recognition of complementary strands: lessons regarding machine learning abilities in RNA folding

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling, cutoff, or wrong-document problem; the full 19-page preprint text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps neural-network capacity and measures test accuracy, a different task and setup from the cited double-descent work. Its results bear on how test performance changes with capacity, but it does not explicitly report a fall-rise-fall curve.
record.gate_note: Capacity sweeps and test-accuracy outcomes are reported for several neural-network architectures. The text does not identify an interpolation threshold or report that test error falls, rises to a peak there, then falls again. The sample-size experiments do not establish the near-interpolation condition in V3. Epoch-wise behavior and the effective-complexity, noise/regularization, and parameter-count explanations are not tested.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps small three-layer networks (log10 C ≈ 2.7–5.5) on a synthetic RNA-complementarity task. It reports test accuracy only as heatmaps and line plots. The text never locates an interpolation threshold, never describes a peak followed by a second descent, and never frames results in double-descent terms. Belkin et al. is cited once, about a random forest fitting noisy training data while generalizing. The text only says 'overfitting behavior is observable' above log10 C ≈ 4 and that higher capacity 'tends to yield better performance'. Neither statement lets anyone judge whether test error falls, rises, then falls again. It also cannot be read whether models reach zero training error. The capacity sweeps measure the right quantity, but the reported results cannot show whether any version holds, so no verdicts are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add the authors' finding that networks struggle to grasp base complementarity, especially in length-wise extrapolation, partly because of zero-padding. Add that scarce examples limit ML for RNA folding. The authors draw no conclusion about double descent.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic RNA complementarity classification rather than the original studies' settings; varies architecture capacity and dataset conditions, with accuracy averaged over simulations.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with task setting and architecture: length-wise extrapolation differs from same-length testing; MLP/CNN outperform Att/LSTM in the extrapolation discussion; for CNN with mislabels in extrapolation, the stated best capacity changes with training-set size.

fits_no_version.finding: A random forest fits 100% of training data that is 20% mislabelled, yet reaches over 99% test accuracy. The authors cite Belkin et al. for this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpolating ensembles can generalize despite fitting label noise (benign overfitting), on this synthetic task.

fits_no_version.finding: Low-capacity nets (log10 C ≈ 3.5) exceed 1−µ test accuracy more often than high-capacity nets (≈5.5) when trained with mislabels; high capacity helps length-wise extrapolation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The best capacity depends on the task: lower for noisy labels, higher for extrapolation.

fits_no_version.finding: Extrapolation with 20% mislabels needs N ≥ 2000 to exceed 80% test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample-size requirement for noisy-label extrapolation in a synthetic RNA task.

record.problems: The experiments use a synthetic, restricted RNA-complementarity task with sequence lengths capped at 8; the authors caution that same-length results may be optimistic. Several relevant capacity results are shown only in figures, and error bars are omitted in Fig 5. The study does not report an interpolation threshold or explicit double-descent curve.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for other sample-size settings or positivity-rate sweeps were included because they do not test the near-interpolation condition in V3 and are not needed to record the reported capacity sweeps. Classical ML comparisons use selected/default or grid-searched settings rather than a reported model-capacity sweep relevant to these versions.

untested.parts: Location of the interpolation threshold, the test-error peak and the second descent; all are figure-only or unreported.
All; training length is fixed at 8×10^4/N epochs and no epoch curves are shown.
All; N sweeps are reported only as monotone improvement, with no near-threshold analysis.
All; classical ML methods (KNN, SVM, tree, forest) are not swept over capacity.
All; label noise µ=0.2 is used, but not as a driver of a peak, and weight decay and dropout are fixed.

missing.what: Capacity sweep at N=500, L=6, µ=0.2, α=0.4. Text: capacity has 'a low impact', with 'slight improvement' as capacity increases. No row records it.

record.verdict_notes: The capacity sweeps use fixed weight decay (1e-3) and dropout (0.1), and the largest log10 C is 5.5. The training-set size at which each model interpolates is never reported, so the interpolation threshold cannot be located from the text. Reading the heatmaps directly might allow V1 states to be assigned; until then all capacity rows are cannot_determine.

versions.untested_parts: Capacity/test-accuracy sweeps are reported, but the text does not establish the full fall-rise-fall shape or locate a peak at the size that just fits training data.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported.
Training-set sizes are varied, but no near-interpolation threshold is identified or tested.
Capacity is varied across four neural-network architectures, but the general claim across model classes and the post-interpolation second descent are not established.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated as a predictor of peak location.

The study varies mislabeling in some experiments, but does not test whether double-descent peaks are caused by noise or variance, split into multiple peaks, or disappear with optimally tuned regularization.
